extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance for mathematicians on collaborative norms, publishing (preprints vs journals), refereeing, grant applications, giving talks, graduate teaching, directing Ph.D. theses, and professional travel. Emphasizes professional behavior, presentation, and administrative/practical rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorship practices (alphabetical authorship and equality)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical collaborations are democratic endeavors, and all the participants are equals. The custom (unlike in other sciences) is to list the authors alphabetically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not squabble over priorities; contributions may vary paper-to-paper; focus on contributing and deriving value from the collaboration. If a collaboration doesn't work out, part amicably.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collaborator moral support and contribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Part of your job as a collaborator is to provide moral support (and praise, when appropriate) for your co-workers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain ideas to teammates, say a kind word for valuable observations, lend a hand when appropriate. Some parts of work will be difficult/tedious; supporting colleagues is part of the role.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect disparate skills
rubrics_metrics.description: Everyone brings something different: some are good at concepts, others at calculation, writing, or asking critical questions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respect and appreciate collaborators' differing strengths and what they contribute to the project.

rubrics_metrics.name: Courtesy and avoidance of divisiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: Everyone should bend over backwards to be courteous to everyone else.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid being critical, demanding, captious, or divisive; keep focus on the joint endeavor and common goal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choosing collaborators carefully
rubrics_metrics.description: Exercise care in choosing your collaborators; prefer people you like and who share interests and goals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid known bad actors; choose collaborators with whom you're compatible to increase likelihood of a happy team effort.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of preprint servers (arXiv) and rapid dissemination
rubrics_metrics.description: Posting on Internet preprint servers (canonical: arXiv) is simple and gets your work out rapidly and broadly; there are no restrictions on posting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preprints are useful for quick dissemination (e.g., Seiberg/Witten example), and you may post on multiple servers or departmental sites.

rubrics_metrics.name: Difference between preprints and peer-reviewed publication
rubrics_metrics.description: Posting a preprint is in a technical sense publishing, but recognized, refereed journals provide validation and carry weight for tenure and promotion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Peer review serves as a filter and stamp of approval; for career advancement, publication in refereed journals matters to deans and committees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Archiving considerations (electronic vs hard-copy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Traditional hard-copy journals are archived in many libraries; electronic media need careful backup and redundancy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Electronic copies can be mirrored/backed-up but are less stable; archiving strategies require redundancy and attention to long-term preservation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Referee's role and desirable tone
rubrics_metrics.description: A referee determines whether a paper/book ought to be published and helps the author with writing, scholarship, and mathematics; do this constructively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even though refereeing is often blind (anonymous), exercise dignity and restraint; be helpful rather than simply castigating the author.

rubrics_metrics.name: Key referee evaluation questions (concise checklist)
rubrics_metrics.description: A good referee’s report should tell the editor some of the following things: Is this paper/book timely? Is it interesting? Is it correct? Is it written in an attractive manner? Are the references complete and accurate? Are the graphics well-rendered? Is the length suitable? Is the result sufficiently important to be published? Is this author the right person to have written this piece?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You may include errata, typos, English corrections, suggested references or alternative proofs. Use these core questions as the primary evaluative filter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detailed referee considerations for long/significant papers
rubrics_metrics.description: For longer papers or those claiming significant results, the referee should also consider whether this is the best approach, whether a more efficient proof exists, how the paper relates to existing literature, whether content justifies length, completeness of references, quality of the introduction and historical overview, organization and readability, clarity of statements and proofs, and the significance of the results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Address these points in greater depth for major submissions; several pages of detailed analysis may be appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate referee report length
rubrics_metrics.description: A referee’s report should be of a length suitable to the task: a short paper can have a short report; a significant result may require several pages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Say what needs to be said—no more and no less; tailor depth to the importance and complexity of the work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Referee timeliness and professional obligation
rubrics_metrics.description: Referees must be timely; a report that takes years is unhelpful to authors and editors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you cannot meet the editor’s deadline, decline the job; if you accept, strive to meet the deadline—this is a professional obligation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grant proposal prose: clarity and accessibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Make your grant writing shine: clear, concise, compelling, complete, and accurate. Proposals are often read by administrators and cross-disciplinary reviewers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid overly technical exposition; provide extra explanation, background, and examples to bring non-expert reviewers up to speed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow granting-agency technical rules exactly
rubrics_metrics.description: Most granting organizations have strict formatting and content rules (margins, font, section lengths, topics); failure to comply can get your proposal returned unread.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adhere strictly to all stated technical requirements of the funding agency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Align proposal with the funding agency’s priorities
rubrics_metrics.description: You must find out what the funding agency is after and speak to those needs (e.g., NSF wants cutting-edge basic research with broad impact; DOE wants energy-related work; Department of Education seeks educational goals).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tailor the proposal narrative to the agency’s mission; describe how the project fulfills their priorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextualize your work: describe milieu and prior results
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe how your contribution fits into the ongoing flow of frontline research, give careful descriptions of previous and partial results (yours and others'), and detailed references.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show you know the subject inside out, the implications of your work, and planned future investigations—funders want to see a coherent program.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be ambitious but realistic in project goals
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposals should be impressive and ambitious but also realistic given the PI’s track record; avoid implausible overclaims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set goals commensurate with prior productivity and the resources requested; reviewers penalize unrealistic promises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grant punctuality and deadline awareness
rubrics_metrics.description: Granting agencies set strict deadlines (or target dates); missing them usually means your proposal will be returned unread.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan time to prepare, review, and finalize the budget; treat deadlines as firm unless explicitly noted as flexible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seek experienced reviewers and allow time for budget preparation
rubrics_metrics.description: Have a senior academic (preferably someone with review-panel experience) vet your draft; allow time to work with departmental staff on the complex budget.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listen to feedback and allot extra time (perhaps a week) to hammer out budget details; budget prep often involves multiple administrative layers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know your audience when giving a talk
rubrics_metrics.description: Tailor the talk to the audience (faculty at top research institutions, MAA meeting attendees, undergraduates, etc.), whose backgrounds and expectations differ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Meet the audience halfway: choose level, examples, and terminology appropriate to their background.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know your subject matter thoroughly
rubrics_metrics.description: Prepare definitions, key results, an outline of main topics, and sources; you should generally know more about the topic than anyone else in the room.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Have succinct notes to avoid stumbling; be ready with definitions and references if requested.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organize the talk to build audience readiness
rubrics_metrics.description: Bring the audience up to speed before presenting new ideas: introduce notation/definitions, give meaningful examples and pictures, and orient with an outline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use both auditory and visual elements; introduce needed terminology before use and provide motivating examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Punctuate talks with milestones
rubrics_metrics.description: Structure the talk with important illustrations, examples, memorable results, key ideas, definitions, or applications to create a compelling flow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid a dreary monotone—use style and content to provide momentum and highlight key transitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practice and rehearse presentations
rubrics_metrics.description: Practice extensively; rehearsing aloud and, for important talks, in front of a small audience is recommended.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Run through notes, work through junctures, and solicit critical feedback from trusted colleagues to craft an effective presentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use physical presentation media effectively (blackboard/overhead/Beamer)
rubrics_metrics.description: Learn how to use your chosen medium: write legibly and visually on boards, do not stand in front of what you write; design effective overheads or slides and pace them properly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid over-dense on-screen PDFs; aim for slides with few lines, large type, and good spacing. If using technology, check the room in advance and rehearse with equipment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Slide pacing and content density
rubrics_metrics.description: Slides should not be dense: about six lines per slide in very large type and spaced; pace at roughly one slide per minute as a rule of thumb.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid flipping through many detailed pages of a paper; give audience time to read and internalize each slide to prevent getting lost.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't present full technical proofs in talks
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid attempting to present full definitive proofs of technical theorems; instead direct explanations to special cases or restricted versions and give indications of the proof strategy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State a pivotal lemma (without proof), draw pictures, indicate key techniques, do an illustrative calculation, and discuss consequences—your job is to convey understanding, not to teach the full proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Honor time limits and prepare graceful exits
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not run overtime; prepare exit points in your talk to wrap up within the allotted time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Running over shows disorganization and is rude; plan a well-timed conclusion and be ready to stop at the prescribed time (typically ~50 minutes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide a clear and satisfying conclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: Conclude by drawing ideas together, reviewing main points, reiterating the substance of the main result, and pointing to future directions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give the audience something to take home and mull over—avoid weak endings like 'I'm out of time' or 'That's all, folks.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Graduate course teaching and preparation
rubrics_metrics.description: Graduate teaching can align with research and lead to new ideas, books, collaborations; preparation varies if good texts exist or if material must be developed from original papers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be prepared to invest time when developing new material; advanced courses can be rewarding but require attention to student recruitment and departmental enrollment rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualifying-exam level courses audience considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Qualifying-exam courses (real analysis, complex analysis, abstract algebra, geometry, etc.) have a known audience and are usually serious and determined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Know the audience's level and expectations; for classes with students from other disciplines (e.g., finance), be ready for more hand-holding and different preparation levels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Directing a Ph.D. thesis: commitment and compatibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Directing a Ph.D. thesis is a huge multi-year commitment involving weekly meetings, mentoring on research life, and often responsibility for future job placement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Get to know the student first (through courses, reading courses, seminars); assess compatibility, check the student's record, talk to colleagues, and take the decision seriously.

rubrics_metrics.name: Directing a Ph.D. thesis: workload and rewards
rubrics_metrics.description: Directing a thesis can be very rewarding but is time-consuming; it may reduce your personal research output but can lead to new papers and lifelong collaborations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weigh the time demands against the potential scholarly rewards; many advisors find the relationship worth the effort.

rubrics_metrics.name: Professional travel as an academic perk
rubrics_metrics.description: Professional travel allows meeting people and seeing new places and is one of the notable perks of academic life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publishing and recognized work lead to invitations to visit or speak; travel can enhance professional and personal life.
